EmoRSS: Mitigating Emotion-Induced Over-Refusal in Large Language Models

Emotional wording can make benign requests look unsafe. EmoRSS steers refusal-related activations to reduce that distortion.

Miao Shuyi

October 4, 2026 ·Preprint ·3-minute read ·Read the paper ·PDF
1Why this matters 2How it works 3What the study finds 4What this means

The short version

EmoRSS investigates why emotional expression can push benign requests toward refusal. Paired queries isolate the change in expression, and sparse autoencoder features connect that change to a refusal-related subspace. The method then reverses the estimated shift during inference while keeping the underlying model frozen.

The study evaluates benign assistance and harmful-request refusal together. This matters because a lower refusal rate is useful only when it reflects better calibration of legitimate requests, while preserving the model’s ability to reject harmful ones.

2Language models evaluated
SAERefusal-subspace features
FrozenNo backbone parameter updates

Safety calibration depends on distinguishing harmful intent from the emotional form of a legitimate request.

Why this matters

Safety decisions should depend on the requested action as well as its context. Benign queries can be unnecessarily refused when emotional expression increases refusal tendencies.

How it works

  1. Locate a refusal-sensitive layer with linear probes and construct an SAE-based refusal subspace.
  2. Compare paired regular and emotional versions of the same queries to estimate a mean feature shift.
  3. Decode that shift into a hidden-state vector and intervene in the reverse refusal direction without backbone updates.

What the study finds

Experiments on two LLMs jointly examine harmful-request refusal, benign-request answering, and general performance. The reported trade-off is more favourable than the compared over-refusal mitigation baselines under emotional wording.

What this means

Helpful safety requires sensitivity to what a user is asking for and stability to how that need is expressed. Emotional distress can be part of a legitimate request; treating that expression as a substitute for risk can systematically withhold assistance from the people who need it.

By connecting a behavioral disparity to an intervenable internal direction, this work offers a mechanism for studying that calibration. Its scope is defined by the tested models and paired-query settings, motivating broader evaluation across emotions, tasks, and conversational contexts.
